title: The elements of theatre at work in a scene
source:
The extract below describes a moment in an original practice scene, 'The Waiting Room'.

It is 4:00 a.m. in a rural clinic. MAVIS, a market vendor in her fifties, sits alone on a bench. A single bare bulb flickers. Every few minutes she stands, walks to the door, looks out, and returns to the bench, folding and unfolding the same cloth. The only sound is a radio in the next room playing a hymn, which fades whenever the door opens. When the NURSE enters at last, Mavis does not speak: she holds out the cloth, the nurse takes it, and they stand facing the audience for a long pause before the lights go out.
prompt: This paper is written theory. Answer ALL parts in writing: plan your answer, write it out in full, then compare it with the model answer and the mark scheme and give yourself the marks you can justify.
planningHints: The elements of theatre are the building blocks a theatre maker chooses from: plot, theme, space, characters, dialogue, rhythm, movement, spectacle, audience and mood.

When a question asks you to explain how an element is USED, name the element, point to what in the extract shows it, and say what effect it has on the audience. A list of elements with no evidence earns only the recall marks.

Some elements are carried by the actor (movement, rhythm), some by the design (space, lighting, spectacle) and some by the writing (plot, theme, dialogue). Draw your examples from more than one of these.
The audience is not a passive receiver: the performance is shaped by the people watching it, which is why the syllabus calls it an element of theatre.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State what is meant by the term 'elements of theatre', and list FOUR of the elements of theatre arts.
markScheme: 1 mark for a clear statement that the elements of theatre are the basic components or building blocks of a performance, or the raw materials from which a production is made.

2 marks for any FOUR correctly named elements of theatre arts, awarded as 1 mark for two correct elements and 2 marks for four (do not accept production elements such as costume, lighting or set on their own - they are elements of production, not of theatre arts).
Do not award a mark for a list of six or more elements that includes anything that is not an element of theatre or production.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain how TWO of the elements you named are used in the extract from 'The Waiting Room' to create the mood for the audience.
parts.modelAnswer:
1. Rhythm and movement. The extract gives Mavis a repeated pattern of action - she stands, walks to the door, looks out and returns to the bench, folding and unfolding the same cloth - and it is repeated 'every few minutes'. That slow, circular rhythm and the small, contained movements make time feel as though it is dragging, and the audience reads waiting, worry and helplessness in it. Nothing is rushing, so the audience's own sense of time slows with hers and the mood becomes anxious and heavy.
2. Sound and space (with spectacle). The only sound is the hymn on the radio in the next room, and it fades every time the door opens, so the sound comes and goes as the hope of the door opening comes and goes; the bare bulb flickering in a plain rural clinic makes the space feel cold and institutional. The quiet, the fading music and the single bulb build tension rather than release, and the audience waits with the character.
Those elements work together, and the writer also uses the pause at the end: after the nurse takes the cloth, the two characters stand facing the audience in silence before the lights go out. The silence is not empty - it makes the audience supply the meaning, which is a strong way of fixing the mood of grief or relief at the very end.
markScheme: 1 mark for each element correctly named, with a point from the extract that shows it (2 marks for two elements).
1 mark for explaining the effect of each element on the audience, in terms of mood (2 marks maximum).
Accept any two of rhythm/movement, sound, space, spectacle, lighting, dialogue/silence, provided the candidate names the element, points to the evidence and states the effect. Maximum 4 marks.
Cap the answer at 2 marks where the candidate names elements but gives no evidence from the extract: the marks are for the use of the elements in this scene.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain why the audience is counted as one of the elements of theatre rather than simply the people who happen to be watching.
parts.modelAnswer: The audience is counted as an element of theatre because a performance does not exist without it and is shaped by it while it is happening. The performers can hear the audience breathe, laugh, shift and go quiet, and they adjust their timing, their voice and their energy to the response they are getting; a pause that is held while an audience is tense works differently from the same pause in an empty hall. The audience also completes the meaning of the work: in 'The Waiting Room' the long silence at the end only means something because the watching audience supplies the feeling of it, and the playwright writes with that response in mind. Finally, the audience is what makes the event theatre rather than a rehearsal - the presence of live spectators, gathered in one place at one time with the performers, is part of the art form itself.
markScheme: 1 mark for stating that a performance is shaped by the audience while it happens - the performers respond to the live reaction and adjust timing, voice or energy.
1 mark for stating that the audience completes or creates the meaning of the performance (for example the silence at the end of the extract is given its meaning by the audience).
1 mark for stating that the live presence of spectators, together with the performers in one place at one time, is what makes the event a performance rather than a rehearsal.
Do not accept answers that only say the audience pays for the show or makes the actors nervous, unless a point about the live shaping of the performance is also made.

examinerTips: Recall earns a little; use earns the rest. Every time you name an element, attach it to something that happens in the extract and then say what it does to the audience. Keep production elements (costume, set, lighting) separate from the elements of theatre arts (plot, theme, character, space, dialogue, rhythm, movement, spectacle, audience, mood) - the syllabus distinguishes between them.

title: Choosing and using a performance space
source:
Hillview Secondary's drama club must choose a space for two different pieces in its end-of-term showcase.

PIECE ONE is an intimate two-hander: a mother and her daughter sorting through a suitcase of family papers. The club wants the audience to feel that they are in the same small room as the two women, and the director wants the audience to be able to see every flicker of the daughter's face.

PIECE TWO is a big, loud celebration piece built on drumming, a procession and more than forty performers, which the club hopes to play to three hundred people a night.

THE THREE SPACES ON OFFER
Space X: the school hall, where the audience sits in rows on raked seating on one side of a raised stage with a decorative arch, a front curtain and wings at both sides.
Space Y: the paved courtyard at the centre of the school, where the audience sits on benches on all four sides and the performers use the middle.
Space Z: a plain drama studio with black walls, a flat floor, flexible seating for about sixty people and a full lighting rig.
prompt: This paper is written theory. Answer ALL parts in writing: plan your answer, write it out in full, then compare it with the model answer and the mark scheme and give yourself the marks you can justify.
planningHints: Name the type of space before you talk about it: proscenium arch, arena or theatre in the round, thrust, black box studio, street or promenade.

Advantages and disadvantages belong to the PRODUCTION, not to the space in the abstract: a proscenium arch hides the scene changes and can seat a big audience, but it puts the audience far from the performers.
The audience's relationship to the action is the key idea - whether the audience is looking at the action through a frame, sitting around it, or inside it.
A recommendation earns its marks from the reasons: name the space, name the piece, and give the evidence from the brief that makes the space fit.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Identify the type of performance space described as Space X and as Space Y, and state ONE feature of the black box studio, Space Z.
parts.modelAnswer:
Space X is a proscenium arch stage (proscenium theatre): the audience sits on one side only, facing a raised stage framed by an arch, with a front curtain and wings. It is formal, end-on staging.
Space Y is an arena stage, also called theatre in the round: the audience is arranged on all four sides and the playing area is in the middle, so the action is surrounded by the spectators.
Space Z, the black box studio, is a flexible space that can be arranged in any way the production needs: it has plain black walls, a flat floor, a full lighting rig and seating that is not fixed, so it can be set end-on, in the round or as a thrust as the piece requires.
markScheme: 1 mark for identifying Space X as a proscenium arch (or proscenium) stage.
1 mark for identifying Space Y as an arena stage or theatre in the round.

1 mark for a correct feature of the black box studio: flexible or movable seating, a flat undivided floor, plain black walls, a full lighting rig, or the fact that it can be arranged in any staging configuration.
Do not accept 'a big hall' or 'a stage' for Space Z: the mark is for the studio's flexibility or its black-box character.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Compare the proscenium arch stage (Space X) with the arena stage (Space Y) for PIECE TWO, the celebration piece with drumming, a procession and over forty performers. Give ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage of each space for this piece.
parts.modelAnswer:
Proscenium arch (Space X), advantages for the celebration piece: it seats a large audience - which is exactly what is wanted for three hundred people a night - and the height and depth of the stage plus the wings allow a large company to be grouped and to make impressive entrances; the procession can move on from the wings across the stage, and the arch frames the drumming group so that the audience's attention is concentrated on one big picture.
Proscenium arch (Space X), disadvantage: the audience sits at a distance and in one direction only, so the celebration is something they watch from outside rather than something they are inside, and the performers at the back of the stage can be far away from the nearest row; a procession that needs to move through people cannot use the auditorium.
Arena stage (Space Y), advantage: the audience surrounds the action, so the celebration becomes an event they are part of; a procession can move through the whole playing area and be seen from four sides, and the drumming builds a shared rhythm between performers and spectators.
Arena stage (Space Y), disadvantage: the performers must play to four audiences at once and must keep turning, so no single spectator sees the whole picture and a group of forty has to be arranged so that every side gets a view; in an outdoor courtyard the drumming and voices may carry and the light cannot be controlled, and the space may not seat three hundred.
markScheme: 1 mark for a valid advantage of the proscenium arch for this piece (large seating capacity, wings and stage depth for a big company, a framed and concentrated picture, the procession entering from the wings).

1 mark for a valid disadvantage of the proscenium arch for this piece (the audience is remote and on one side only, the celebration is observed rather than shared, the audience cannot be used as part of a procession).

1 mark for a valid advantage of the arena for this piece (the audience surrounds and shares the event, the procession can travel through the space and be seen from all sides, the drumming creates a shared rhythm).

1 mark for a valid disadvantage of the arena for this piece (the company must play to four sides at once, no one spectator sees everything, the arrangement of forty performers is difficult, and in an open courtyard the light can not be controlled and three hundred seats may not be available).

Maximum 4 marks. Award the marks only where the point is tied to this production; a general advantage of a stage with no reference to the forty performers, the procession or the audience of three hundred earns no mark.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Recommend which space the club should choose for PIECE ONE, the intimate two-hander, and justify your choice with TWO reasons.
parts.modelAnswer:
I recommend Space Z, the black box studio, with the seating arranged on three sides as a shallow thrust, or on two sides facing each other.
Reason 1: intimacy and the audience's relationship to the action. The director wants the audience to feel that they are in the same small room as the two women, and the studio seats only about sixty people, so the nearest spectators are within a few metres of the actors; in a studio the audience is not separated from the acting area by a raised stage and an arch, so the imaginary wall of the room can run right through the audience and they become the fourth wall rather than onlookers in a hall.
Reason 2: control of the detail. The studio has a full lighting rig on a flat floor, so the flicker of a face can be isolated with a close, soft spot or a special, which is what the director asks for; the black walls let the audience see nothing but the two women and the suitcase, and the flexible seating means the suitcase can be placed at the centre of the audience's attention. A proscenium stage in a school hall would put the two women at a distance, and the courtyard would expose the piece to daylight and to an audience on all four sides, which prevents the sense of a private room.
markScheme: 1 mark for recommending the black box studio (Space Z) as the space for the two-hander.
1 mark for the first reason, supported by the brief: the studio's small capacity and lack of a raised framed stage make the audience intimate with the two performers, which the director wants.
1 mark for the second reason, supported by the brief: the lighting rig and plain black walls can isolate the daughter's face and hold the audience's attention on the suitcase and the two women.
Accept a well-argued recommendation of a different space only where the candidate answers the two briefs - intimacy and the visible face - and explains how their chosen space provides them.

examinerTips: Name the staging form first (proscenium, arena/theatre in the round, thrust, black box, street, promenade), then argue from the production's needs: capacity, the audience's relationship to the action, sightlines, entrances and the control of light. Marks are lost by praising a space in general terms instead of showing why it suits THIS piece - the two-hander wants closeness and a visible face; the celebration wants room for forty performers and a procession.

title: The theatre company, the production process and safety
source: The Baytown Players, a community theatre group, is mounting an original play in the school hall in six weeks' time. The group has a director, a stage manager, an actor-manager who also performs, a lighting and sound operator, a costume team of two parents, three front-of-house volunteers and a cast of twelve, most of whom are secondary-school students who have never been on stage before. The hall is also used for lessons every day, so everything has to be struck and stored after each rehearsal.
prompt: This paper is written theory. Answer ALL parts in writing: plan your answer, write it out in full, then compare it with the model answer and the mark scheme and give yourself the marks you can justify.
planningHints: Theatre personnel are the people who make the production happen, on stage and off; each role has tasks and each role answers to another role, which is how the company is organised.
The production process runs in stages, from choosing the play and auditioning, through rehearsal and the technical and dress rehearsals, to the performance run and the strike.
A safety answer must be practical and tied to this hall - a space shared with lessons, used by young and untrained performers, with cables, ladders, darkness and a get-out each night.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State the main responsibility of the director, of the stage manager and of the lighting and sound operator in this production.
parts.modelAnswer:
The director is responsible for the artistic whole of the production: interpreting the play, deciding the concept and the style, working with the actors on character, blocking, pace and meaning in rehearsal, and approving the design and the look of the show so that all the elements serve the intention of the piece. In this company the director must also integrate the twelve untrained performers into the world of the play.
The stage manager is responsible for the organisation of the production off stage: the running of rehearsals and the performance, the prop and furniture tables, the calling of the cues, the rehearsal schedule and reports, the prompt copy, and - important here - the safety of the space and of everyone in it, including the strike and storage of everything after each rehearsal, since the hall is used for lessons every day.
The lighting and sound operator is responsible for the technical effects that the design calls for: plotting and focusing the lights, running the lighting and sound desk during the performance, calling or taking the cues at the right moment, checking that the microphones and speakers work, and keeping the cues safe and repeatable so that each performance is the same.
markScheme: 1 mark for the director's responsibility: the artistic interpretation and shaping of the production, working with the actors and approving the look of the show.

1 mark for the stage manager's responsibility: organising and running rehearsals and performances, calling cues, keeping the prompt copy and the rehearsal schedule, and managing the safe state of the stage.
1 mark for the lighting and sound operator's responsibility: plotting and operating the lighting and sound, taking the cues at the right time and keeping each performance consistent.
Do not accept a role with no responsibility attached, or the actor's task given as the director's task.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Outline the stages of the production process the Baytown Players would follow from the first planning meeting to the strike, and say what is decided or achieved at each stage.
parts.modelAnswer:
1. Planning and selection. The group chooses the play and the date, confirms the budget and the hall booking, decides the production team and the design approach, and sets the rehearsal schedule around six weeks and a hall that is in daily use.
2. Casting and preparation. Auditions and recalls are held, the cast and the roles are confirmed, and the design and technical work begins: costumes measured, props collected, the set planned around what can be stored and struck each night.
3. Rehearsal. Blocking and character work, then running the acts, then the whole play; lines are learned, the pace is fixed, and the actors get used to the set, the props and the entrances and exits.
4. Technical and dress rehearsals. The lights and sound are focused and plotted, cues are recorded in the prompt copy, the scene changes are timed, the costumes and make-up are tried in performance conditions, and the first audience of invited guests tests the whole event.
5. Performance run and strike. The company performs the scheduled shows, with the stage manager calling cues and the front of house running admissions; then, after the last performance, everything is struck, returned, cleaned and stored and the hall is handed back ready for lessons, and the company holds a review of what worked and what did not.
markScheme: 1 mark for each correct stage with what is decided or achieved there - planning and choice of the play (budget, dates, production team), casting or preparation (auditions, design, props and costumes), rehearsal (blocking, character, running the acts), technical and dress rehearsals (focus and plot of lights and sound, cues, costume in performance), performance run, and strike and review - maximum 4 marks.
Accept 'audition', 'rehearsal' and 'performance' as stage names only when the candidate says what happens at that stage; a bare list of stage names earns no more than 2 marks.
Do not award a mark for a stage given out of order without comment, or for 'the show' as a stage.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain TWO health and safety measures the company must put in place for this production, and say what each measure prevents.
parts.modelAnswer:
1. Managing cables, set and the get-out. The hall is used for lessons every day, so the set pieces must be struck and stored after each rehearsal and the cables to the lights and sound equipment must be taped down or run in a cable ramp, and no trailing lead may cross an exit route or a walkway. This prevents a member of the public, a student or an actor from tripping in the dark and prevents a lamp or a speaker being pulled over during a scene change. The person doing it is the stage manager, who also checks before every rehearsal that the space is safe and that nothing has been left in the way.
2. Lighting the working areas and training the young cast. The hall is not a theatre: the backstage area, the wings and the route from the dressing space to the stage must have enough light to be walked safely while the stage itself is dark, and the twelve untrained students must be shown how to move on and off, how to handle props and how to behave in a blackout before they are asked to perform it. This prevents falls and collisions in the dark, burns and cuts from unfamiliar props, and the panic that can spread through a cast that has not been prepared. Other correct measures: a fire exit kept clear and the front-of-house team briefed on evacuation, a first-aid kit and a named first aider, safe working at height with a second person holding the ladder, and no eating or drinking near the lighting desk.
markScheme: 1 mark for each valid safety measure, clearly described and tied to this hall and this company (2 marks for two measures).
1 mark for stating what the measure prevents - a fall, an electric shock, a burn, a collision or an injury to the audience or the cast.

Maximum 3 marks. Accept measures such as taping or ramping cables and clearing exits, lighting backstage routes, lighting the get-in and strike, training the inexperienced cast, a first aider and a first-aid kit, safe use of ladders, and keeping the hall usable for lessons.
Do not accept a general statement such as 'be careful' or 'follow the rules' with no measure attached.

examinerTips: Keep the roles distinct - the director shapes the art, the stage manager organises and runs the production, the technicians plot and operate the effects. In the process question, give five stages in order and say what is decided at each: choice of play, casting and preparation, rehearsal, technical and dress rehearsal, performance and strike. A safety answer must name the measure, say who carries it out and say what it prevents; tie it to the shared school hall with its cables, darkness and daily get-out.

title: Staging a Caribbean cultural form
source:
The Mandeville Youth Theatre Company is taking part in a community heritage programme. For its twenty-minute piece the company has chosen to build the performance around a Caribbean cultural form, and after research it has narrowed the choice to TWO:

OPTION 1 - Kumina, the Jamaican tradition of the parish of St Thomas, with its drumming and dancing, inherited from the Bakongo people of Central Africa, in which the community honours its ancestors.

OPTION 2 - Ananse and the Pot of Wisdom, the storytelling tradition in which the spider trickster, Ananse, is used to teach and to make people laugh, told in the language of the people and handed down from generation to generation.

The company's notes record that the piece will be performed on a raised platform on the edge of the community field, in daylight, for an audience of families and visiting councillors. The leader of the company has warned the cast that they must not perform the form as though it were decoration: they must know what it means to the people who keep it.
prompt: This paper is written theory. Answer ALL parts in writing: plan your answer, write it out in full, then compare it with the model answer and the mark scheme and give yourself the marks you can justify.
planningHints: Start from the definition: a cultural form is a traditional practice - a way of singing, drumming, dancing, telling stories or marking an occasion - that is passed on in a community and carries the meaning of that community.

Physical elements are what you can see and hear: movement, rhythm, drumming, song, dress, props, the space and the people. Symbolic elements are what those things MEAN: the ancestors, the community's history, healing, celebration, respect or protest.

Influence on Theatre Arts means the transfer of skills and structures: movement vocabulary, rhythm as structure, call-and-response with the audience, improvisation, and staging outside the theatre building.

The last part is about respect and accuracy. In its own setting the form belongs to the community and is done for its own purposes; staged, it is performed for an audience. Say what changes and why the research matters.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Define the term 'cultural form' and name THREE Caribbean cultural forms with the territory or territories each one is associated with.
parts.modelAnswer:
A cultural form is a traditional practice of a community - a way of singing, drumming, dancing, telling stories, playing a game or marking an occasion - that has been handed down through the generations and that carries the meanings, the history and the beliefs of the people who keep it. It is learnt by taking part in it, and it belongs to a community rather than to an individual artist.
Three Caribbean cultural forms and their territories:
1. Kumina - Jamaica, particularly St Thomas.
2. Landship - Barbados.
3. Stick fighting (kalinda) - Trinidad and Tobago.
markScheme: 1 mark for defining a cultural form as a traditional practice handed down in a community, carrying that community's meaning, belief or history.
1 mark for naming - correctly - TWO cultural forms with their territories, and 1 mark for a THIRD (maximum 2 marks).

Accept any of Kumina (Jamaica), Landship (Barbados), stick fighting or kalinda (Trinidad and Tobago), Nansi or Anansi storytelling (Jamaica), Carnival (Trinidad and Tobago and the wider Caribbean), ring games (across the Caribbean), wakes or nine-night (Jamaica and the wider Caribbean).
Do not accept a form with the wrong territory, or a form that is not Caribbean, or a named religion with no form attached.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Choose the form the company should use - Kumina or Anansi storytelling - and describe the physical elements and the symbolic elements of that form.
parts.modelAnswer:
I choose Kumina, the Jamaican tradition of St Thomas.
Physical elements. Kumina is carried by drumming: two or more drums, the lower drum keeping the rhythm and the lead drum playing the calls that the dancers answer, joined by shakers and sometimes by a metal gong. There is singing in call-and-response, with a lead singer or 'queen' giving the line and the group answering, and the music builds from a slow opening to a fast, driving peak. The dancing is grounded and rhythmic - steps on the spot, circling, and the whole body answering the drums - and the dancers wear clothing in the colours of the tradition, sometimes white, and the ground they dance on is prepared and treated as a special space, often in a yard with a table or a corner set aside. The people are arranged around the drummers and the dancers, with the community watching and taking part.
Symbolic elements. The drum is not just an instrument: it is understood as the voice of the community and as a way of speaking to the ancestors, and the ceremony is kept to honour them, to give thanks, to heal, and to ask for protection. The whole form stands for the memory of a people brought from Central Africa and for the survival of that inheritance in the Caribbean; it stands for the community's unity, its respect for those who have passed on, and its identity as a people who keep their own tradition alive. Its performance is also a form of knowledge: the elders pass on the songs and the steps to the young, and so the tradition is itself a way of teaching who the community is.
markScheme: 1 mark for choosing one of the two forms.

1 mark for a physical element correctly described - drumming, call-and-response singing, grounded rhythmic dancing, dress, the prepared dance space, the arrangement of the community around the performers (accept a second physical element for a further mark, maximum 2 marks).

1 mark for a symbolic element correctly explained - the drum as the voice of the community or a way of speaking to the ancestors, the form as memory of an African inheritance, as thanksgiving, healing or protection, as community unity, or as a way of passing knowledge to the young (accept a second symbolic element for a further mark, maximum 2 marks).

For Anansi storytelling: the physical elements are the voice, the improvisation, the audience's answers, the language, the gestures and the place of telling; the symbolic elements are the trickster as survival and wit, the handing on of wisdom and the community's own voice.
Do not award the descriptive marks for a list of names only: the candidate must say what the element is and what it does.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain TWO ways in which a Caribbean cultural form of your choice has influenced Theatre Arts in the Caribbean.
parts.modelAnswer:
1. Movement and rhythm as the basis of staging. Theatre makers in the Caribbean have taken the grounded, drum-led movement of forms such as Kumina, Landship and Carnival and used it as the physical language of a production: the dance steps, the circling and the answering of the drum become the movement vocabulary of a scene, and the drum pattern becomes the structure of the scene itself - the action rises to the peak of the drum rather than to the peak of a spoken speech. That is an influence of form on the art, because the rhythm is organising the drama rather than decorating it.
2. Audience participation and the use of space. In forms such as Anansi storytelling, ring games and Carnival the audience is not silent and separated: it answers the teller, joins the chorus, claps the rhythm and moves with the procession. Caribbean theatre has taken that participation into its own practice - performers speak directly to the audience, songs invite an answer that the audience knows, and companies play in yards, on the street and in market squares instead of only in a theatre building. The effect is a theatre in which the community is inside the performance, and the boundary between performers and audience is deliberately broken.
A third influence, if needed: the form provides its own repertoire of stories, characters and heroes (the trickster, the ancestor, the ship's crew of the Landship) and its own music, which playwrights and choreographers use as the raw material of new theatre works.
markScheme: 1 mark for each correct influence explained, with the form it comes from and what it changed in theatre practice (2 marks).

1 mark for each well-supported detail of HOW that influence works in performance - for example rhythm organising the structure of a scene, movement vocabulary supplying the physical language, call-and-response breaking the barrier with the audience, or playing in non-theatre spaces (2 marks).
Maximum 4 marks. Accept influences drawn from Kumina, Landship, Carnival, stick fighting, Anansi storytelling or ring games, provided the candidate ties the form to a change in theatre practice.
Do not accept a general statement that 'our culture is in our theatre' with no named practice and no explanation of what changed.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Justify why the company must study the form carefully before staging it, and state ONE difference between the form in its authentic setting and the form in a staged performance.
parts.modelAnswer:
Justification. A cultural form is not simply a style that can be copied: it is a living practice that belongs to a community, and it carries meaning for the people who keep it. If the company performs it without knowing that meaning, it risks three things. First, it can misrepresent the form - the wrong drum pattern, the wrong step or the wrong dress turns a serious tradition into an imitation, and the audience that knows the form will see it at once. Second, it can give offence: a form used for honouring ancestors or for healing may not be performed carelessly or for entertainment alone, and parts of it may not be for public display at all. Third, the research makes the piece better art: the research gives the company the form's real movement, music, language and meaning, and a performance made from understanding is more truthful and more powerful than one made from a video. In this programme, where families and councillors are watching, the company is also representing the community's heritage, so accuracy is part of the company's responsibility.
One difference between the authentic setting and the staged performance. In its own setting the form is done by the community, for itself, for its own purpose - thanksgiving, mourning, healing, remembrance or celebration - and the people present are participants rather than an audience, with no fixed beginning or end and no tickets. On a stage it becomes a performance for people who are watching: the duration is fixed to fit a programme, the sequence may be shortened or re-arranged, the dance may be taken out of its ceremonial order, and the performers are acting on behalf of the tradition rather than taking part in it. A further difference, if needed: in the authentic setting the form takes place in its own space and time - the yard, the crossroads, the night before a burial - while the staged performance here uses a raised platform, in daylight, for an audience that has come to watch a programme.
markScheme: 1 mark for a valid justification - the form belongs to a community and carries its meaning, so performing it without knowledge misrepresents it (accept accuracy, respect, avoiding offence, not treating it as decoration).

1 mark for a further, well-supported justification - the research makes better art, or the company is representing the community's heritage to an outside audience (maximum 2 marks for the justification).

1 mark for a correct difference between the authentic setting and the staged performance - participation for the community's own purpose compared with performance for watching strangers; the form's own setting and time compared with a stage; no fixed length compared with a fixed programme slot (maximum 2 marks for two differences, 1 mark for one).

Maximum 4 marks. Do not award the justification marks for 'so that we do it properly' with no reason; and do not accept as a difference the fact that the stage is indoors while the form is outdoors, which is true here but is not the essential difference.

examinerTips: Define the form as a living practice of a community before you describe it, and keep the physical elements (drumming, song, movement, dress, space) separate from the symbolic ones (ancestors, memory, thanksgiving, identity). Influence on Theatre Arts is about transfer: rhythm as structure, movement as language, call-and-response as participation, and playing outside the theatre building. The last part of this question is really about respect and accuracy - say what the research protects the company from, and say clearly what changes when the form moves from its own setting onto a stage.

title: Analysing an extract from a Caribbean play
source:
The extract below was written for this practice paper by the makers of CSEC Compass. Read it carefully and answer the questions that follow.

RAIN ON THE ZINC ROOF - a scene for two actors

A yard in the hills. Evening. A mango tree, one chair, an old sheet of zinc leaning against the wall. NELLA, sixteen, sits on an upturned bucket. CEDRIC, her father, stands at the edge of the light. The rain on the zinc roof is heard throughout.

CEDRIC. The rain coming again.
NELLA. It is the same rain, Papa.
CEDRIC. (Pause.) Is the same rain.
NELLA. When they take the tree, is not the same yard. When they take the zinc, is not the same house.
CEDRIC. They say is for the road. Everybody getting a road.
NELLA. And we getting a promise.
CEDRIC. (Crossing to the zinc, touching it.) Your mother cut this zinc with she own two hand. You hear that? That is she voice in the rain.
NELLA. (Standing, taking the zinc from him, holding it in both arms.) Then I will carry she voice. But Papa - I will choose the road.
CEDRIC. (Quietly.) Choose it good, then.

The church bell is heard, far off, under the rain. NELLA holds the zinc; CEDRIC sits on the chair at last, facing the house. Neither moves. The rain stops.
prompt: This paper is written theory. Answer ALL parts in writing: plan your answer, write it out in full, then compare it with the model answer and the mark scheme and give yourself the marks you can justify.
planningHints: A text analysis answer needs evidence. Say what the character or device does, then point to the line or the stage direction that shows it, then say what effect it has.
The functions of characters include moving the plot, revealing theme, opposing or supporting another character, giving the audience information, and standing for something larger than themselves.
Dramatic devices to look for: repetition, silence and pause, the symbolic object, off-stage sound, contrast, the stage direction, the direct address and the choice of language or dialect.

Production elements are the designer's and director's tools: set and props, lighting, sound, costume and make-up, movement and staging. Say how you would use them AND what you want the audience to feel.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State the function, or functions, of Nella in this extract, and support your answer with evidence from the lines she speaks.
parts.modelAnswer:
Nella carries more than one function in the extract.
She is the character who drives the action and the argument forward. Her father opens with a statement that the rain is coming again, and it is Nella who turns that into the play's real subject: 'When they take the tree, is not the same yard. When they take the zinc, is not the same house.' She names what is being lost and forces her father to answer, so the scene moves from the weather to the sell-up of the land.
She also carries the theme of the scene - the choice between memory and the future. Her last two lines, 'Then I will carry she voice. But Papa - I will choose the road,' set the memory of her mother beside her own decision to leave, and the play's argument lives in that sentence.
She is also the character who gives the audience the information they need: through her we learn that the tree and the zinc are going, that there is a road coming, and that the family has been given a promise instead of payment.
Finally, she both supports and opposes her father: she takes the zinc from him gently ('Then I will carry she voice') and immediately contradicts him ('But Papa - I will choose the road'), so she keeps the relationship alive while she stands against his position.
markScheme: 1 mark for naming a function of Nella - she drives the action or the argument forward, she carries the theme, she gives the audience information, or she opposes and supports her father - with a line from the extract as evidence.
1 mark for a second function, again supported by a line.
1 mark for a third function, or for showing how the functions work together in this scene (for example that she supports her father emotionally while she opposes him in argument).
Maximum 3 marks. Award no mark for a function with no evidence; a mark may be awarded where the function is explained with a clear reference to the lines even if the line is not quoted word for word.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Analyse ONE thematic concern of this extract and explain how the writer develops it through the words and the stage directions.
parts.modelAnswer:
The main thematic concern of the extract is the conflict between memory and the future - between holding on to what has been and choosing to move on.
The writer develops it through the argument between father and daughter. Cedric speaks for memory: for him the rain and the zinc are the same because his wife is in them - 'Your mother cut this zinc with she own two hand. You hear that? That is she voice in the rain.' The stage direction 'Crossing to the zinc, touching it' shows that his attachment is physical: he holds on to the object because he cannot hold on to the person. Nella speaks for the future: 'is not the same yard', 'we getting a promise', 'I will choose the road'. The two positions are set side by side in single lines of dialogue, so the theme is not explained to the audience but argued out in front of them.
The writer also develops the theme through objects and through the structure of the ending. The zinc is both a roof and a person - it is the thing that must go and the thing that must be carried, and Nella's taking it into her arms in the stage direction turns the argument into an image: she will keep the voice and still leave. The last three stage directions - the church bell, 'NELLA holds the zinc; CEDRIC sits on the chair at last, facing the house', 'The rain stops' - settle the theme without a word: the past is honoured, the decision is made, and the storm inside and outside the yard is over. The theme is therefore carried by the whole apparatus of the play, not only by what the characters say.
markScheme: 1 mark for stating a valid thematic concern - memory against the future, the loss of home or land, inheritance and the handing on of memory, the pressure of development, or a daughter's independence (accept any one, clearly stated).
1 mark for a point of evidence from the dialogue, correctly used to support the theme.

1 mark for a point of evidence from the stage directions (the zinc touched, held or carried; the pause; the bell; the rain stopping; the father sitting and facing the house) and an explanation of what it adds.

1 mark for explaining HOW the writer develops the theme - through opposing positions in single lines, through a symbol, through the structure of the ending, or by leaving the resolution to the images rather than the words.
Maximum 4 marks. Do not award the development mark for a re-telling of the story, or for the theme with no evidence at all.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Evaluate TWO dramatic devices used in the extract and explain the effect of each one on the audience.
parts.modelAnswer:
1. Repetition and the deliberate echo. The rain is 'the same rain' three times - twice as a statement and once as Cedric's agreement, 'Is the same rain' - and the zinc and the tree are named again and again. The effect is to make the audience listen to a small change inside a repeated phrase: what begins as an observation about weather becomes a statement about loss, and the moment Cedric repeats his daughter's words the audience hears that he has understood her. Repetition also slows the scene down, so the audience feels the weight of the decision rather than the speed of it.
2. The symbolic object, carried and held. The sheet of zinc is worked on three times - it leans against the wall, Cedric touches it as though it were his wife, and Nella takes it into both arms. By the end the object is not scenery: it is the mother, the house and the inheritance at once, and because the audience has watched it being handled with care, they accept the meaning without the playwright having to name it. The image also gives the audience the one visual fact they will remember: a girl carrying a piece of roof.
A third device, if needed: the pause and the silence. The stage direction '(Pause.)' before Cedric's agreement, and the wordless ending under the church bell, make the audience lean into the silence to find the feeling; silence after an argument is louder than any line the writer could give the characters. The off-stage sound of the rain and the bell adds the world beyond the yard, so the private decision is heard against the life of the village.
markScheme: 1 mark for naming a dramatic device used in the extract (repetition, silence or pause, the symbolic object or prop, off-stage sound, contrast, stage direction, dialect, direct address) and 1 mark for the effect of that device on the audience - the second device with its effect earns the further 2 marks (maximum 4 marks).
1 mark is available within each pair for evidence from the text that shows the device at work.

Maximum 4 marks. Do not award a device more than once; 'good dialogue' or 'nice stage directions' is not a device. An effect must be described in terms of what the audience understands, feels or anticipates.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain how you would use TWO production elements to stage this extract, and state what you want the audience to feel at the end of it.
parts.modelAnswer:
1. Sound. The rain is written into the extract and runs under every line, so I would build the whole scene on a live, low rain sound on the roof - not a general effect but a specific, intimate sound, close enough to be heard in the silences. I would keep the level almost constant so that the audience stops hearing it, then, at the end, take it away on the line 'The rain stops' and let the church bell come up from far off in the dark. The effect is that the audience feels the yard go quiet with the decision: the storm that carried the mother's voice is over, and what is left is the bell and the house.
2. Set, props and lighting. The set is a yard at evening: a real mango tree branch, one chair, an upturned bucket and the sheet of zinc leaning against the wall. I would light it with a warm, low side light that picks out the zinc when it is touched, so the light moves with the father's hand and then finds Nella as she takes the zinc into her arms; the rest of the stage stays in a soft gloom, and the father's face falls out of the light as he sits and faces the house, so the audience reads his surrender in lighting before anyone speaks. Costume would be simple and worn - work clothes, bare feet - so the audience sees a family and not a display.
What I want the audience to feel: I want them to feel the ache of the decision and, at the same time, respect for it - that a daughter can carry her mother's voice out of the yard and still be right to take the road. I want them to leave the theatre in silence, holding the picture of the girl with the piece of roof.
markScheme: 1 mark for each production element named and explained with a specific choice (sound; set, props and lighting; costume and make-up; movement, blocking and staging) - 2 marks for two elements.
1 mark for each element showing a clear intended effect on the audience or a reason for the choice (maximum 2 marks).

1 mark is available for stating what the audience should feel at the end - for example the ache of the decision mixed with respect for it, or the stillness of the yard - provided it is tied to the choices made in the answer.
Maximum 4 marks. Do not award a mark for naming a production element with no choice attached ('I would use lighting'); the marks are for how the element is used and why.

examinerTips: Every answer here should follow the same shape: name it, prove it from the text, then say what it does to the audience. Functions of characters, themes, devices and production elements are four different questions - keep them apart. The stage directions are part of the text and are often worth more than the dialogue: the pause, the zinc handled three times, the church bell and 'The rain stops' all carry the meaning of this scene.
